strengths: The paper presents a useful and reasonably original systems/methodological idea: approximate molecular embeddings by additive synthon-level contributions, then exhaustively stream all combinatorial products through a GPU top-k operator. This exploits CSL structure and supports changing objectives and constraints after precomputation.

The 12M-compound exhaustively scored benchmark enables direct measurement of top-j recall, rather than relying solely on enrichment metrics. Across five targets and several constraint sets, Figure 3 shows substantial gains over random selection, while Figure 8 indicates generally competitive recall against Thompson sampling.

The scalability result is practically significant: Table 1 reports searches over more than 10B products in roughly 11–24 seconds on a single T4 GPU, including constrained queries and k up to one million.

The methodology is presented clearly, with an explicit optimization problem, factorization equations, and a useful description of the CUDA chain-of-batches implementation. The authors also disclose that their generated library is not guaranteed to be synthetically feasible and state that code, datasets, and weights are provided.
weaknesses: The central claim that screening the 10B library finds better compounds is not validated with the true expensive objective. Only the 12M library is exhaustively docked; Figure 4 appears to compare surrogate-selected or surrogate-predicted score distributions for the 10B set. Selecting extreme predictions from a much larger pool can amplify surrogate error, so redocking at least the retrieved 10B candidates is essential before concluding that larger-library screening identifies genuinely better-scoring molecules.

The data-splitting protocol raises a serious leakage concern. Section 2.1 describes the 1M and 12M libraries as products of downsampling the same reactions and then trains on the 1M library while evaluating on the 12M library. It does not state that their products are disjoint. If the 1M library is nested in the 12M library, evaluation directly includes training compounds; calling this a remedy for leakage is incorrect. Results should be reported on an explicitly disjoint product split, ideally with held-out synthons or reactions as a harder generalization test.

The Thompson-sampling comparison is not fully apples-to-apples. APEX benefits from one million labeled docking evaluations used to train its surrogate, whereas matching k only to the evaluations made during each TS run omits this substantial label cost, as well as factorizer training and precomputation. Amortization across queries is a valid advantage, but the paper should separately report initialization costs and comparisons under both per-query and total-label budgets.

Surrogate quality for docking is only moderate and target-dependent: Figure 7 suggests factorized R-squared values of roughly 0.3–0.6 for the five docking endpoints. Yet the paper provides no repeated splits, uncertainty estimates, calibration analysis, ranking metrics, or error analysis of extreme-tail candidates, where top-k screening is most sensitive. Figure 3 alone therefore gives limited evidence for robustness.

The benchmark is only an analogy to a make-on-demand CSL: it recombines BRICS fragments and explicitly does not ensure synthetic feasibility. This materially limits the practical significance of the drug-discovery claims and the comparison with commercial synthesis-on-demand libraries. Evaluation on at least one realistic reaction-validated CSL would considerably strengthen the work.

Reproducibility details in the manuscript are incomplete despite the promised artifacts: surrogate and factorizer architectures, sampling procedures, optimization settings, training cost, random seeds, and memory usage are not adequately reported. The runtime table also labels query execution as end-to-end while excluding model training and precomputation.

Several conclusions overstate what is supported. Exhaustive enumeration applies only to the factorized approximation, so statements that valuable compounds are not overlooked are unwarranted when the surrogate can misrank them. Likewise, docking-score enrichment is not evidence of biological activity. The limitations discussion should more clearly address model error, applicability domain, synthetic feasibility, docking limitations, and potential chemical dual-use considerations.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: repeated constrained search over extremely large combinatorial libraries. Fast amortized querying could be valuable in early-stage virtual screening.

The additive factorization of surrogate embeddings is clearly formulated and naturally enables efficient enumeration. The custom GPU top-k implementation appears practically useful, with reported query times below 30 seconds for one million results from the 10-billion-entry library on a Tesla T4.

The exhaustively scored 12-million-compound benchmark spans five protein targets and several constraint sets, enabling ground-truth retrieval evaluation at a scale larger than many molecular-optimization studies.
On the 12-million-compound library, APEX substantially outperforms random selection and generally matches or exceeds the tested Thompson-sampling baseline, particularly at smaller budgets.
The main method is presented coherently, and the distinction between expensive molecular scoring, surrogate prediction, and factorized surrogate prediction is mostly clear.
weaknesses: The central ultra-large-scale accuracy claim is not convincingly validated. Only the 12-million-compound library is stated to have exhaustive docking labels, yet Figure 4 reports docking-score distributions for APEX selections from the 10-billion-compound library without explaining whether these compounds were independently docked. If these are APEX or surrogate predictions, the enrichment result is circular; if they were docked, the protocol and sample size are missing. Thus the paper demonstrates 10-billion-scale execution, but not reliable 10-billion-scale retrieval.

The split construction raises a serious leakage concern. The 1-million training library and 12-million evaluation library are described as uniform downsamplings of the same reactions, apparently nested within the same 10-billion library. The manuscript does not state that training compounds are removed from evaluation, and synthons and reactions are heavily shared. This setting mainly measures interpolation among known components and may even include direct compound overlap, despite the claim that it addresses leakage.

The baseline comparison is too limited and budget accounting is unfavorable to Thompson sampling. It covers only five reactions, only unconstrained search, and matches the baseline's expensive evaluations to APEX's output size while omitting the one million labeled docking examples used to train APEX. Relevant hierarchical, active-learning, nearest-neighbor, and unfactorized-surrogate baselines are absent.

Reported query times exclude major amortized costs: generation of the million labeled training examples, surrogate training, factorizer training, preprocessing, and cached-contribution construction. Training time, peak memory, storage, and break-even query count are not reported, so the practical end-to-end scalability claim cannot be assessed.

The benchmark explicitly does not ensure synthetic feasibility, although the motivation centers on make-on-demand synthesis libraries. BRICS-valid recombination is not evidence that products can actually be synthesized or purchased. This substantially limits the benchmark's realism and the claimed drug-discovery significance.

Surrogate quality is uneven: Figure 7 shows modest or poor R-squared for several docking endpoints, particularly ESR1 and F10, with additional degradation after factorization. Correspondingly, Figure 3 shows limited recovery in several stringent/top-ranked settings. The paper does not analyze ranking calibration, replicate uncertainty, feasibility false-positive rates near constraint boundaries, or how factorization error changes retrieval relative to the original surrogate.

The claimed robustness from adding embedding noise and its connection to the errors-in-variables problem are asserted rather than theoretically established or supported through ablations. There is no comparison without noise, across factorization ranks or embedding dimensions, or against direct additive property models.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the hierarchical reaction factorizer is explicitly adapted from Pedawi et al. (2022), while the main new elements are its use for surrogate ranking and the optimized top-k implementation. The paper does not sufficiently isolate which gains arise from the proposed factorization versus the pretrained surrogate and engineering.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits essential surrogate and factorizer architectural details, optimization settings, sampling seeds, docking parameters, preprocessing choices, and complete hardware/software specifications. The code footnote is blank in the supplied manuscript, and no data-access details or artifact validation are available here.

There is no substantive limitations or broader-impact discussion. The manuscript should explicitly address docking-score unreliability as a proxy for binding, possible generation of infeasible or undesirable molecules, domain shift to commercial libraries, and the need for independent computational and experimental validation. Figure 8 is also too small to inspect reliably, and several conclusions overstate 'high recall' and assurance that valuable compounds are not overlooked. These evidential and reproducibility deficiencies outweigh the promising systems idea.

strengths: Soundness: The core factorization is technically plausible and clearly derived: linear task heads allow each compound score to be expressed as a sum of cached synthon-level contributions, enabling exhaustive enumeration and exact top-k retrieval with respect to the factorized surrogate.

Evaluation: The fully enumerated 12M-compound benchmark provides genuine ground-truth top-j sets for five docking objectives and several constraint regimes. APEX shows substantial recall and constraint enrichment over random selection and generally matches or exceeds Thompson sampling on the tested reactions.

Significance: Fast, declarative, constraint-aware search is useful for repeatedly querying very large combinatorial libraries. The reported end-to-end query time—about 24 seconds for one million results from over 10B candidates under Lipinski constraints on a T4 GPU—is practically impressive.

Originality: Combining a reaction-aware latent factorization with exhaustive GPU top-k search offers a meaningful new screening workflow, even though parts of the hierarchical representation build on Pedawi et al. (2022).

Presentation: The paper is readable, well structured, and explains the CSL hierarchy, factorization, and CUDA search strategy clearly. Figures 3, 7, and 8 expose performance across endpoints rather than reporting only an aggregate.

Reproducibility and limitations: The authors construct an open benchmark rather than relying on a proprietary CSL, state that the generated compounds are not guaranteed synthetically feasible, specify the docking software, targets, constraint definitions, hardware, and embedding dimension, and claim release of code, datasets, and weights.
weaknesses: The Thompson-sampling comparison does not appear compute- or label-budget matched. APEX first consumes labels for the entire 1M-compound training CSL, including target-specific docking scores, whereas the baseline receives much smaller per-reaction evaluation budgets; matching only APEX's output k to the number of TS evaluations understates APEX's expensive upfront supervision. Results should include total-cost comparisons and amortization curves over numbers of subsequent queries.

The strongest 10B-library quality claim is not validated with ground-truth docking. Figure 4 reports favorable score distributions for APEX-selected compounds, but the 10B predictions may reflect surrogate extrapolation or selection-induced overoptimism. Docking a substantial random subset of the retrieved candidates, and reporting precision/enrichment against those true scores, is needed to establish that larger-library retrieval finds genuinely better candidates.

The paper reports only online query runtimes. It omits the wall-clock time, hardware, sample count, and memory cost for generating 1M labels, training the surrogate, training the factorizer on each library, and precomputing associative contributions. These costs are central to the practical value and claimed amortization of the method.

Generalization is tested on a 12M library derived by expanding the same reactions and synthon pools used to create the 1M training library. This is a relatively favorable interpolation setting; performance on new reactions, new building blocks, or a realistic commercial CSL remains unknown. The benchmark also deliberately does not ensure synthetic feasibility, limiting the drug-discovery conclusions.

Factorized prediction quality is uneven: Figure 7 shows modest R-squared values for several docking targets and very poor performance for some structural properties. The manuscript gives no uncertainty estimates, repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or ablations of factorizer capacity, embedding noise, training-set size, and factorization error. In particular, the claimed robustness supplied by embedding noise is asserted rather than experimentally demonstrated.

Important implementation details are absent from the manuscript, including surrogate and factorizer architectures, training schedules, sampling distributions, split construction and deduplication, hyperparameters, and docking-protocol details. The anonymous code link is not visible in the provided PDF, so reproducibility cannot be verified from the submission alone.

The conclusions overstate the evidence by saying exhaustive screening ensures that valuable high-scoring compounds are not overlooked. Enumeration is exhaustive only under the approximate factorized surrogate; errors in docking itself, the surrogate, and the factorizer can still exclude the true best compounds. There is also no experimental binding validation.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations or broader-impact discussion. Ethical risk is limited for this methodological study, and LLM use is disclosed, but chemical dual-use considerations and the distinction between predicted docking scores and experimentally useful drug candidates deserve explicit treatment.

strengths: Originality/significance: The additive factorization of surrogate embeddings over reaction-specific synthon contributions is a clever application of structured retrieval to combinatorial libraries. It enables exact top-k retrieval under the factorized approximation and supports recombining previously trained endpoints into new constrained queries without retraining.

Soundness: The method is clearly formulated, including the surrogate, factorizer, constrained lexicographic top-k procedure, and error decomposition. On the fully scored 12M library, APEX substantially exceeds random retrieval and often matches or outperforms Thompson sampling on the five tested reactions.

Efficiency: The custom GPU implementation demonstrates impressive measured throughput: constrained top-1M retrieval from 10B products takes about 24 seconds on a Tesla T4, while a 70B REAL-library search takes roughly three minutes.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover five targets, multiple drug-likeness constraints, factorization error, counter-screening, composite objectives, two library scales, and a zero-shot Enamine REAL application. The appendix provides useful architectural and training details.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear. It makes no unsupported claim of experimental biological validation, and I see no unresolved material ethical concern in conducting computational virtual screening.
weaknesses: The comparison does not account for APEX's dominant upstream cost. APEX uses a 1M-compound labeled training library—apparently requiring docking one million molecules for every new protein target—whereas Thompson sampling is compared at budgets of only thousands to tens of thousands of oracle evaluations. Calling the downstream shortlist size a matched 'evaluation budget' therefore produces an inequitable efficiency comparison. Surrogate/factorizer training time, sampling volume, preprocessing cost, and amortization break-even point are not reported.

The empirical baseline coverage is insufficient for the central performance claims. Aside from random selection, the only competitive baseline is Thompson sampling, evaluated separately on merely the five largest reactions (about 4M of the 12M products), without constraints. The cited pool-based active-learning, deep-docking, hierarchical, or dense-retrieval approaches are not tested, so the claim of consistently strong performance relative to alternatives is only weakly supported.

The fully evaluated 12M benchmark is derived by downsampling the same BRICS reaction system as the 1M training library. The manuscript does not precisely state whether the two enumerations overlap or quantify shared synthons/products. Even without product overlap, this mainly tests unseen combinations of familiar reaction components. The Enamine experiment helps, but it offers only enrichment against a random background—not ground-truth recall or a competitive baseline—and shows substantial zero-shot R-squared degradation for some endpoints.

The benchmark is described as a combinatorial synthesis library even though the authors explicitly do not ensure synthetic feasibility. BRICS recombination is structurally analogous to a CSL but does not validate performance on genuinely make-on-demand chemistry. This weakens the drug-discovery significance of the principal ground-truth experiment.

Recall is useful but moderate: at k=100,000 (0.803% of the 12M library), top-100 recall is roughly 0.6–0.77 without constraints and commonly about 0.2–0.5 under stronger constraints. Constraint satisfaction is also substantially imperfect for several rule sets. The conclusion's language about ensuring that valuable compounds are not overlooked is consequently too strong.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although architectures and some optimizer settings are reported, the paper omits the exact construction/splitting relationship among the 1M, 12M, and 10B libraries, factorizer sample counts and fine-tuning details for the 10B library, training compute and duration, random seeds, uncertainty across training runs, and docking validation details. The displayed code URL is incomplete, so the promised code, data, and weights cannot be verified from the manuscript.

Several technical statements need qualification: encoding cost is called logarithmic in library size although that does not follow generally from the CSL formalism; robustness to errors-in-variables is asserted from embedding-noise training without theoretical or ablation evidence; and the trillion-product timing argument is FLOP-based while largely ignoring memory bandwidth and top-k overhead.

Limitations are not treated adequately. The paper should explicitly discuss docking-score reliability, domain shift, false positives under surrogate constraints, the absence of synthetic feasibility in the benchmark, target-specific labeling expense, dependence on additive factorization, and the distinction between fast computational ranking and therapeutic discovery. These omissions and the unfair cost comparison currently outweigh the promising core idea.

strengths: Originality/significance: The reaction-aware additive factorization is a clever application of structured retrieval to combinatorial synthesis libraries. Caching per-synthon contributions enables practically important query-time scaling, with measured searches over 10B and 70B compounds on one T4 GPU.

Soundness: The 12M-compound exhaustively scored benchmark permits direct measurement of top-j recall rather than relying only on surrogate regression metrics. Evaluation spans five targets, several constraint sets, and both two- and three-component reactions.

The paper usefully separates surrogate and factorization errors and reports rank correlations, constraint satisfaction, retrieval recall, and runtime. The CUDA implementation appears to be a substantive engineering contribution.

Presentation is generally clear, with a coherent formalization and helpful architectural and implementation details. The authors also candidly state that their BRICS library is not guaranteed to be synthetically feasible; this honest limitation should not itself be penalized.
The proposed benchmark, docking labels, code, and weights could be valuable community resources if the promised releases are complete and usable.
weaknesses: Soundness: The comparison with Thompson sampling is not budget-equivalent. APEX first consumes up to 800,000 labeled training molecules, including target-specific docking labels, whereas the plotted TS budgets count its oracle evaluations directly. Restricting TS to five reactions while APEX benefits from globally trained representations further complicates the comparison. Thus the claim of superior low-budget screening is not supported by a fair accounting of expensive oracle calls.

The headline runtimes omit the dominant preprocessing costs: generating 1M labeled molecules, training the surrogate, training or fine-tuning the factorizer on each library, and computing cached contributions. No training times, factorizer sample counts, or amortization break-even analysis are given. Calling the reported search time “end-to-end” is therefore misleading for a new screening endpoint or library.

The claimed flexibility is overstated. Queries can only use the 28 endpoints for which linear heads were trained; a new target-specific docking objective requires new labels and surrogate training, followed by factorization. This is materially narrower than arbitrary on-the-fly objectives and constraints.

The evaluation split is insufficiently specified and potentially leaky. The 1M and 12M libraries are created by downsampling the same reactions, apparently share synthons, and may even contain overlapping products. The paper does not report overlap removal or harder held-out-synthon/reaction splits. Performance therefore mainly demonstrates interpolation within one constructed BRICS system, not generalization to new chemistry.

Evidence on true vendor-scale CSLs is weak. The Enamine experiment is zero-shot on a proprietary library, uses only a 100,000-molecule background, and does not report sample sizes or uncertainty for the accuracy measurements. Enrichment against a random background does not establish recall of the unknown true top compounds.

The synthetic benchmark explicitly does not ensure synthetic feasibility, despite the motivating advantage of make-on-demand CSLs. Results on this construction may not transfer to real reaction templates, and the paper evaluates only docking scores from one computational pipeline, without prospective or experimental validation.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. Beyond the problematic TS comparison, there is no controlled comparison against active-learning screening, Deep Docking-style filtering, V-SYNTHES, a simple additive per-synthon predictor, or other scalable surrogate/indexing approaches. The unfactorized surrogate curves show that factorization often loses recall, but the associated speed–accuracy tradeoff is not quantified.

Reported recall is only moderate despite rhetoric such as “consistently achieves high recall”: at k=100,000 on 12M compounds, Figure 2 shows substantial target- and constraint-dependent miss rates, particularly for larger top-j sets. No confidence intervals over model training seeds are supplied.

Some theoretical/scaling statements are inaccurate or unsupported. Encoding in O(|S|+|R|+|T|) is described as logarithmic relative to O(|D|), which is not generally true, and the trillion-compound “few seconds” discussion ignores memory bandwidth, enumeration, and top-k overhead; empirical 70B searches already take roughly three minutes.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the code claim: essential settings such as embedding-noise magnitude, factorizer training-set size/sampling, batch sizes, stopping/model-selection rules, random seeds, and preprocessing costs are deferred or absent. The proprietary Enamine experiment is not independently reproducible from the manuscript.

Limitations and ethics are treated too narrowly. The impact statement discusses only benefits and omits risks from docking-score error, false confidence in approximate constraints, accessibility of proprietary libraries, and potential misuse. Overall, the method is promising, but these evidential and reproducibility gaps prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Soundness: The additive factorization is technically coherent: linear task heads allow cached per-synthon contributions to be summed, making exhaustive surrogate evaluation over a combinatorial library practical. The custom GPU top-k implementation is well aligned with this structure.

Evaluation: On the exhaustively labeled 12M-compound benchmark, APEX achieves substantial top-j recall at a 100,000-compound budget across five targets and several constraint sets. It generally matches or outperforms the Thompson-sampling baseline at matched oracle budgets.

Significance: The reported end-to-end performance is practically compelling—approximately 24 seconds for a constrained top-1M query over the 10B BRICS library and about 202 seconds over the 70B REAL library on one Tesla T4. Fast re-querying under changed objectives or constraints is genuinely useful.

Originality: Applying an associative, synthon-level factorization to exhaustive constrained retrieval in combinatorial synthesis libraries is a novel and elegant synthesis of surrogate modeling and structured retrieval.

Presentation: The central idea, mathematical construction, implementation strategy, and model architecture are explained clearly. The appendix provides endpoint definitions, constraints, hyperparameters, error decomposition, and per-target results.

Reproducibility and ethics: The paper states that code, data, and weights are available, supplies detailed architectures and optimization settings, and constructs an open benchmark to reduce dependence on proprietary libraries. No major ethical issue is apparent, and the impact discussion appropriately avoids making experimental drug-discovery claims.
weaknesses: Soundness: The strongest accuracy evaluation is confined to a synthetic 12M-compound BRICS library explicitly constructed without ensuring reaction or product synthetic feasibility. This weakens the connection between benchmark retrieval performance and the motivating setting of make-on-demand CSLs.

Evaluation at scale is indirect. For the 10B and 70B libraries, the paper demonstrates docking-score enrichment rather than recall against an exhaustive ground-truth top-k set. The Enamine result is compared with only 100,000 random background compounds, so it does not establish near-optimal retrieval over that 70B library.

The empirical baseline coverage is narrow. Only Thompson sampling is compared directly, only without constraints, and only on the five largest reactions rather than the full library. Pool-based active-learning or surrogate-screening baselines, hierarchical synthon screening, and simpler additive models are discussed but not evaluated.

The learned components lack uncertainty analysis and key ablations. Results appear to come from a single training run, and the manuscript does not isolate the benefit of embedding-noise regularization, factorizer hierarchy, embedding dimension, training-set size, or 10B-library fine-tuning. The claim that noise makes predictions robust to errors-in-variables is asserted without a theorem or controlled experiment.

Generalization is tested under limited distribution shifts: the 1M training and 12M test libraries share the same BRICS construction process and likely reactions and synthons. A split by synthons, reactions, scaffolds, or source molecules would better quantify whether performance extends beyond interpolation within one constructed CSL.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated release. Exact factorizer sampling and fine-tuning amounts, training time and hardware, learned-model variability, library-generation details, and machine-readable numerical results are not fully reported. Reproduction of the 70B experiment may also depend on access to the commercial Enamine library.

Some claims are overstated or imprecise. The conclusion describes recall as consistently high although top-100 recall is roughly 0.3–0.8 depending on target and constraints; the appendix calls O(|S|+|R|+|T|) logarithmic relative to O(|D|), which is not generally true; and the maximization formulation is not explicitly reconciled with minimizing docking scores.

The limitations and impact sections are too brief. They should explicitly discuss docking-score validity, synthetic infeasibility of the BRICS benchmark, surrogate-induced false negatives, restricted commercial-library access, and the need for experimental validation before treating retrieved molecules as plausible hits.
